checkpoints: Logging and error tracking are two separate observability pillars: a call like `logger.error(...)` only appends a line to the central log store, while a grouped issue, captured stack trace, and frequency-based alert are produced by the error-tracking pillar (e.g. Sentry) and only happen when that pillar actually receives the exception.
A `catch` block that logs a failure and returns a fallback value (such as `null`) without rethrowing stops the exception right there — it never propagates further up the call stack.

A framework-level global exception filter (e.g. `SentryGlobalFilter` registered via `APP_FILTER`) only runs for exceptions that propagate up through the request pipeline; if a `catch` block swallows the error and returns normally, the handler looks like a success from the framework's point of view, so the filter never executes and the error tracker never records anything.
Swallowing an exception is not inherently a bug — returning a fallback for a genuinely optional side effect can be the correct design.

The defect in code like this is that a real production incident (e.g. a payment refund silently failing) gets hidden behind a log line and a response that looks successful, with no mechanism to surface that it is happening at scale.
One valid fix is to remove the local `catch` (or rethrow a typed exception from it) so the error propagates naturally into the global exception filter, which then reports it to the tracker.

If returning a fallback truly is the correct behavior for that code path, the alternative fix is to keep the `catch` but explicitly call the error tracker's capture method (e.g. `Sentry.captureException(err)`) inside it before returning the fallback, so the failure is still recorded even though it never reaches the global filter.

Correctness of the fix should be verified by deliberately forcing the failing call to throw and confirming that a grouped issue with a full stack trace appears in the error tracker — not just by checking that a line was written to the log store.

A WAF middleware that inspects only `req.body` leaves the query string, the path, cookies, and headers open — headers such as `X-Forwarded-For` and `Referer` are classic places attackers stash SQLi/XSS payloads precisely because teams often check only the body.
Coverage limited to a single input surface makes a WAF a false sense of security rather than real protection, even when the team believes the API is already "protected."

Echoing the offending payload back inside a 403 response — e.g. `res.status(403).json({ status: 'blocked', input: req.body })` — turns the very control meant to stop injection into a reflected-XSS sink.
A block response should carry only `{ status, rule }` and never a copy of the input that was submitted, since the response itself becomes an attack vector otherwise.

Wiring the middleware with `consumer.apply(WafMiddleware).forRoutes(OrdersController)` instead of `forRoutes('*')` leaves every other controller in the app with zero WAF coverage, not partial coverage.

With no cap on request body size, a very large payload makes the inspection scan run against the entire body, turning the WAF's own inspection step into a CPU/DoS amplifier — the opposite of what a security control is meant to do.

The reflection sink is the highest-priority fix because it's an active vulnerability today, not just a gap; the input-surface gap and the route-coverage gap can be closed together next since both already let attackers sail through untouched; a body-size cap comes last as hardening.

Even a fully-fixed WAF remains a backstop, not a replacement for parameterized queries and output encoding — treating it as the whole defense leaves a team over-trusting a filter that a well-encoded attack can still slip past.
Unwrapping a DEK means sending the wrapped key to a KMS like Vault Transit and getting the plaintext key back over HTTP — each unwrap is a full network round-trip, not a local operation.

Calling `TransitService.unwrapDek` on every single read means the same record's DEK gets re-unwrapped from Vault on every request, even when it was just decrypted moments earlier, so the KMS round-trip dominates read latency.

Looping over N rows and `await`-ing `unwrapDek` inside the loop sequentially turns a batch/list endpoint into an N+1 pattern against the KMS: N records cost N separate HTTP round-trips whose latencies stack up one after another.

Putting the KMS directly on the hot read path also makes it a single point of failure for reads — if Vault slows down or becomes unreachable, every read request fails along with it, not just the writes that actually need fresh key material.

Caching the unwrapped DEK in memory for a short TTL (for example a `Map` keyed by wrapped DEK or record id storing `{ dek, expiresAt }`) lets repeat reads of the same record skip the Vault round-trip entirely until the entry expires.

The DEK cache must live only in process memory and never be written to disk, so a crash or restart loses it exactly as if it had never been cached — this preserves envelope-encryption's bounded blast radius and crypto-shredding guarantees, since the plaintext key never becomes durable outside Vault.

Fixing the N+1 in the batch endpoint means collecting all the wrapped DEKs and sending them in a single request to Vault Transit's batch endpoint (using a `batch_input` array) instead of issuing one `unwrapDek` call per row — this collapses N round-trips into one.

Running Vault Transit in high availability, such as multiple nodes behind a load balancer or Enterprise performance replicas, removes the single-node-failure risk so one Vault instance going down doesn't take every read with it, and the fix should be validated by comparing round-trip counts and p50/p99 read latency before and after, plus a test confirming the DEK cache actually expires at its TTL and is never persisted outside memory.

Calling `repo.find({ order: { index: "ASC" } })` materializes every row of the audit table into memory before the loop even starts, so the endpoint pays a full-table scan on every single request regardless of how many rows were already verified in a prior call.

The verification loop always seeds `expectedPrev` with `GENESIS_PREV_HASH` and re-walks the chain from index 0 on every call, making the cost O(n) in both time and CPU — one hash recomputation per row, every time, no matter how many earlier calls already proved the older entries intact.

A health/monitoring probe hitting this same endpoint every few seconds turns an already-expensive full-scan-plus-full-recompute into continuous, unbounded load on the database as the audit log grows toward tens of millions of rows.

Storing a periodic checkpoint — `{ count, entryHash, anchoredAt }` — written by a background job lets verification start from the last confirmed position instead of genesis, bounding both memory and recompute work to only the rows appended since that checkpoint.

The checkpoint must be mirrored somewhere the application's own database role does not also control — an external notary, a second datastore, or a SIEM — otherwise the checkpoint is exactly as forgeable as the hash chain it is meant to protect.

Streaming rows instead of loading them all with `repo.find()` (e.g., a query-builder `.stream()` returning a Node `Readable`) keeps memory flat regardless of table size; this is a separate fix from checkpointing, which bounds the recompute work rather than the memory footprint.

An internally consistent hash chain cannot detect truncation: if the newest rows are deleted after the last checkpoint, the remaining chain still verifies correctly, so an incremental scan over the surviving tail has nothing to compare against and would wrongly report success.

Catching truncation requires comparing the current tail's count and entryHash against a value anchored externally and independently of the primary datastore — an in-place edit changes a hash, but a deletion of the newest rows just makes the chain shorter, and only an external anchor exposes that difference.

Moving from full re-hash to checkpoint-based incremental verification shifts the trust boundary from the per-row hash to the checkpoint and the witness's independence, so a sparser anchoring cadence widens the window in which an attacker could time an edit and a truncation to land undetected before the next anchor runs.

Vault's KV v2 secrets engine wraps every read response in two nested envelopes: the JSON body is `{ data: { data: {...values...}, metadata: {...version...} } }`, so the actual secret values sit under `response.data.data.data` when read through axios (whose own `.data` holds the parsed body).

A successful `vault kv put` together with a raw HTTP GET against `/v1/secret/data/my-app` returning the value proves Vault itself, the token's read permission, and the original write are all fine, which narrows the fault to how the client code parses the JSON response.

`response.data?.data?.DB_PASSWORD` stops one hop short of the real value: it resolves to the inner envelope object `{ data: { DB_PASSWORD }, metadata: { version } }`, which has no `DB_PASSWORD` key of its own, so the optional chain quietly evaluates to `undefined` instead of raising a traversal error.

The `if (!password) throw new Error(...)` guard is functioning exactly as intended as a fail-fast check — it just cannot tell a genuinely missing secret apart from a response read at the wrong nesting depth, so it throws a misleading "not found" error for what is really a parsing bug.

The fix is one more `.data` hop — `response.data?.data?.data?.DB_PASSWORD` — and the resulting nested chain should not be flattened or "simplified" later, because it mirrors Vault's real KV v2 envelope structure (outer HTTP wrapper, inner data, sibling metadata) rather than being redundant defensive code.

Fetching the secret inside `TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync`'s `useFactory` means a parsing bug in `VaultService.fetchDatabasePassword` surfaces as an application boot crash rather than a contained runtime error, which is why the symptom reads as a startup failure instead of a scoped, easily isolated bug.

The bug can be pinned down and prevented from regressing with a fixture test: feed the function a response shaped like the real KV v2 body (`{ data: { data: { DB_PASSWORD: 'x' }, metadata: { version: 1 } } }`) and assert the extracted value equals `'x'`, plus a second case where `DB_PASSWORD` is genuinely absent and the fail-fast `Error` still throws.
